defects: The longest shot runs 11.2s. It is a slow camera drift over a static sheet, and 7 of 29 seconds barely change from the second before.
Most of the movement is the camera panning, cropping and pulling out over one flat document. The objects themselves hardly move, so there is little weight, overlap or follow-through.
The handwriting reads as a font, not a hand. The checkmarks are near-identical glyphs and the letters keep the same baseline rhythm, which undercuts the premise of hand-filled notes.
The circles do not sit cleanly on their words. The 'still no clip' ellipse cuts through the TR4 checkmark, and the 'got the top' and '30 hrs, one roll' loops collide with text and run off the edge.
Several frames are mid-pan crops that cut words in half ('every ti', 'Te', 'rolls the moment you'), so they do not hold up as stills.
The rain-on-tin-roof row shows a wash of grey light that looks like a soft lighting pass, not designed light. The paper is shaded differently from shot to shot.
There is a 2s full-band white-noise block (about 5.6–7.5s) with a dead-flat top and a hard cutoff. It reads as a placeholder hiss rather than designed sound, and it falls right in the static stretch.
The 'roll' line ('1') and the right-margin fields are cut off at the frame edge in close-ups.
gaps: Choreography: one camera move does the whole film. Top studio work would make the marks perform: an ink stroke with real pressure and speed, a circle drawn hard and fast as a hit, a carbon sheet lifted to reveal the next layer. Each event should hand off to the next, not be panned past.

Pacing and arc: the circled 'got the top / no clip' climax arrives as a gentle reveal with no build or release, and the 11s drift kills the energy. It needs a tighter build through the failed takes (NG, INC, FS), a sharp turn at the switch to 'Tern', and a held, earned settle at the end.

Sound and finish: the soundtrack is busy and evenly dense, with transients everywhere, so cuts and pen strokes cannot land as accents. The noise block sounds like a placeholder rather than tape or room tone. The lettering needs real hand variation and pen-pressure texture to match the paper's material quality.
